questions.q: A customer in Castle Hill asks what happens if your repair leaks again in six months. How should you answer?
options: Tell them everything we touch has a lifetime warranty on it
Say it depends, and they'll need to ring the office to find out
Explain our promise in the approved wording every tech uses
Promise you'll personally come back for free whenever they call
questions.why: Every tech explains the promise the same way, in the approved wording. If one tech invents their own version, the customer hears two different companies.

questions.q: Two techs each finish five jobs in a day around Penrith. Which one had the better day for the truck as a business?
options: The one who fixed each job first time and was paid and signed off before leaving
The one who fitted in a sixth job by leaving the payments for the office to collect
The one who finished early by skipping the health check on the smaller jobs
The one who kept every customer happy by rounding their prices down a little
questions.why: A truck hits its numbers through first-time fixes, the whole problem fixed and every job paid and signed off before you leave. Return trips, unpaid jobs and discounts all cost the truck.

questions.q: Swapping a tap in a Chatswood unit, you close the valve under the sink and the tap keeps running. The next shut-off is the building's main, which affects every unit. What do you do?
options: Work on it wet with towels down, since it's only a quick cartridge swap
Shut the building main straight away so you can finish on time
Ask the customer to hold a bucket under it while you swap it quickly
Stop, photograph the valve and call the office before using the main
questions.why: Never work a valve that won't fully shut off. Go to the next isolation point, and if that affects other people, call the office first.

questions.q: Stepping off a ladder in a Willoughby laundry, you skid on wet tiles. You don't fall and nothing is damaged. What do you do?
options: Nothing to report, since nobody was hurt and nothing in the laundry broke
Report it as a near-miss today, and dry the floor and foot the ladder
Mention it at the next team meeting if it's still on your mind by then
Log it only if the customer saw it happen and might make a complaint
questions.why: A near-miss is when something nearly happened, and you report it just like an incident. It shows us the hazard before someone gets hurt.

questions.q: You're finishing a job in Ryde and heading to your next customer across town. When do you set 'on my way' in ServiceTitan?
options: When you pull up outside the next customer's house
When you actually leave, after calling the customer
At the start of the day for all your jobs, to save time
Once the office confirms the last job's invoice is paid
questions.why: Set 'on my way' when you actually leave, not before and not on arrival, and call the customer before you pull out. Dispatch plans everyone's day from your statuses.

questions.q: You've just finished a bathroom job in Strathfield and taken five good before-and-after photos. The office is usually quick to answer texts. What's the right move?
options: Text them to the office, who'll add them to the job when they can
Keep them on your phone in case the customer queries the job
Email them to yourself and upload them all at the end of the week
Save them to the job in ServiceTitan before you leave the site
questions.why: If it isn't in ServiceTitan, it didn't happen. Texted photos often never make it onto the job, so nobody can find them when the work is questioned months later.

questions.q: Your first job is running over, and you'll be well past the arrival window for a customer in Gordon who took the morning off work. What do you do?
options: Call her yourself before the window passes, and let dispatch know
Push on and apologise when you arrive, since you'll get there soon
Leave it to dispatch to notice and ring her if they have time
Send her a text once you're parked outside so she knows you're there
questions.why: If you're running late, ring the customer before their arrival window passes and tell dispatch so they can adjust the day. A call turns a complaint into a courtesy.

questions.q: Halfway through replacing a shower mixer in Maroubra, you find the pipe behind it is badly corroded. What do you do?
options: Replace the pipe while the wall is open, then add it to the final invoice
Replace the pipe at no charge so the customer isn't upset by it
Stop, photograph it, show the owner her options and get signed approval
Finish the mixer and mention the pipe on your way out the door
questions.why: If something changes once you're into the job, you stop, show the customer, price the options from the pricebook and get signed approval before carrying on. Unapproved extra work breaks the no-hidden-costs promise.

questions.q: You're at a rental in Merrylands on an agent's work order for a blocked toilet. In the laundry, the hot water unit is leaking from the base. What do you do?
options: Leave it, since it's outside what the agent's work order covers
Note it at the bottom of the invoice so the agent sees it later
Tag it hot-water-8yr+ so the office follows it up next month
Tell the tenant, photograph it and flag it 'Needs attention now'
questions.why: Something that risks damage if it's left gets flagged 'Needs attention now' so the office calls the same day. Never tuck it at the bottom of the invoice or decide it's not your job.

questions.q: You're running behind on a vanity mixer swap in Randwick and notice the cabinet floor under the basin is already swollen from an old leak. What protects you best?
options: Take before photos of the swollen cabinet before any tool comes out
Point it out to the customer verbally and get started straight away
Photograph it once the new mixer is in and the job is finished
Leave it out of the notes, since it isn't part of today's job
questions.why: Before photos, taken before a single tool comes out, prove the damage was already there. Once you've started, you can't go back and take them.

questions.q: It's ten to five in Hurstville and you want to beat the traffic. The customer taps their card and the payment fails. What do you do?
options: Leave and let the office sort the payment out tomorrow morning
Close the job as complete and tell the customer you'll text a link
Stay calm, try another method, and ring the office if it fails
Offer a small discount if they can pay you in cash right now
questions.why: A failed payment is the same as no payment. Try another method, check it goes through, and if it can't be sorted, call the office before you leave. Never offer a deal for paying a certain way.

questions.q: You finish a planned job and state the balance. The customer says, "I already paid." What do you do?
options: Take their word for it and close the job in ServiceTitan as paid in full
Check the job in ServiceTitan, then state the balance and collect it
Tell them they're mistaken and ask for the full price again
Leave it unpaid and ask Chloe to sort it out with them next week
questions.why: Check, never assume. It's often a mix-up, like thinking the deposit covered everything. Look at what's actually been paid in ServiceTitan, then state the balance clearly and collect it.

questions.q: You're sent back to a Mosman home where a mixer another tech fitted last month is dripping. What's the right way to handle it?
options: Apologise for the hassle, fix it properly and note what you found
Explain that whoever fitted it last month didn't do it properly
Fix it quickly and leave it off the job record to save time
Tell the customer it isn't your fault and refer them to the office
questions.why: Returns are handled graciously, linked to the original job, with no blaming another tech. Note what you found so the business can learn from it.

questions.q: You sold and captain a planned bathroom job in Epping. On completion day, the customer rings you unhappy about paying the balance. What do you do?
options: Agree a lower balance yourself, since you were the one who sold it
Ask the installer to waive part of the balance to keep them happy
Tell Charlotte straight away, since she owns payment and happiness
Tell them to raise it with Chloe when she makes her happy call
questions.why: As job captain you own the handover, the installer's questions and the finish, but the Install Manager (Charlotte, interim) owns payment and the customer's happiness. Tell her straight away so she can look after it.

questions.q: You're writing the scope for a hot water replacement that means cutting old pipes out of a plaster wall. What must the scope say?
options: Just the new unit's model, since the customer can ask about the rest
What's included, and that patching the wall afterwards isn't
That any extra costs will be worked out on the day of the install
That the wall will be left looking as good as new afterwards
questions.why: Every estimate says what's included and what isn't. A vague scope lets the customer fill the gaps with assumptions that turn into arguments on install day.

questions.q: You're quoting a re-pipe in an older Lane Cove house. The template hours assume easy access, but the subfloor is low and tight. What do you do?
options: Use the template hours as they are, since templates are already tested
Leave the access issue out so the price stays as competitive as possible
Type a higher price over the template line to cover the extra work
Note the tight access in the scope so the hours reflect the real site
questions.why: Realistic hours matter because the installer's time and the business's profit depend on them. Note anything that will slow the job in the scope, and never type your own price.

questions.q: Your camera shows roots in a drain in Dee Why, and the customer is waiting at the kitchen table. How do you build the quote?
options: Type the lines in one by one so the quote fits this job exactly
Quote the clear only, and build the rest back at the depot later
Open the Drain Fix-for-Good template and fit it to what you found
Copy last week's drain quote for another customer and adjust it
questions.why: Never build from scratch when a template exists. Start from the template, then add or remove pricebook lines to match what you actually found.

questions.q: A template you use every week has hours that are clearly too low for how the job is really done. What do you do?
options: Raise it with Harriet so the template gets fixed for everyone
Quietly add a few extra hours each time you use the template
Stop using it and build that job from scratch from now on
Make your own copy with better hours and share it with the team
questions.why: If a template's wording or hours look wrong, don't quietly work around it. Raise it with Harriet (Sales Manager) so it's reviewed and fixed for every quote.

questions.q: A customer in Strathfield watches you replace a tap in under an hour and says, "That's a lot for an hour's work." What's the best reply?
options: Offer to charge them by the hour instead, if they'd prefer that
Agree it's steep, and say you'll ask the office for a better price
Explain it's mostly the cost of the parts, not the hour of labour
Explain the fixed price covers far more than the hour they saw
questions.why: The customer only sees your hour. The price also pays for the booking, the van, the parts on board, the office and the warranty, and offering to ask the office for a better price is a discount by another name.

questions.q: Halfway through a job in Engadine, the old isolation valve won't turn off. You have a new one in the van. What do you do?
options: Fit the new valve quietly, since it's a small part and it helps them out
Stop, show them, price it from the pricebook and get signed approval
Fit it and add it to the invoice, since they'll clearly want it
Fit it and record it as goodwill so it doesn't upset the price
questions.why: Extra work done as a favour either breaks the no-hidden-costs promise or comes out of the profit as unbilled materials. Stop, show the customer, price it from the pricebook and get signed approval.

questions.q: A Carlingford customer with a failing hot water unit hears the price and says, "I need to think about it." What's the best next step?
options: Offer a deal if she's happy to sign before you leave today
Ask whether her worry is the overall cost or whether it's worth it
Say you'll ask the office to sharpen the price and call her back tonight
Leave the quote with her and wait for her to ring when she's ready
questions.why: Stay calm and curious: find out whether the concern is price or value, then clarify the options and the promise. If she still isn't ready, agree a follow-up time and log it.

questions.q: A customer in Kings Langley says another plumber quoted a few hundred dollars less. What do you do?
options: Offer to match the other quote so you don't lose the job to them
Point out that the other plumber's reviews aren't as good as ours
Drop them to a lower option before they've even asked for one
Ask what their quote included, then explain what comes with ours
questions.why: We don't compete on price and we never knock the other plumber or offer to beat a quote. Find out what their quote covered, then walk through what the Proximity promise gives them.

questions.q: In Dundas, a customer says, "Yep, let's do Premium. Just book it in and I'll sign when your installer turns up." What do you do?
options: Get the plan signed in ServiceTitan now, before anything is booked
Book it with Kim and note that the customer will sign on the day
Order the materials now so the job is ready, then book it in
Leave it there, since a clear verbal yes is enough to lock it in
questions.why: A yes at the table isn't approval. The plan is approved when it's signed in ServiceTitan, and nothing is scheduled or ordered until the deposit is in.

questions.q: The installer arrives at a hot water upgrade you sold in St Ives to a locked side gate, a dog in the yard, and no idea where the owner wanted the new unit. What was missing from your handover?
options: The materials list and any special parts to be ordered
The estimated hours and the exclusions in the scope
The access details and the customer's notes
The deposit amount and when the balance is due
questions.why: Every handover covers access (gates, keys, pets) and customer notes (what they want on the day). The test is whether the installer could do the job without ever calling you.

questions.q: You clear a blocked toilet in Gladesville in twenty minutes. On the way out you notice a rusty 12-year-old hot water unit and perished flexi hoses under the vanity. What does doing your whole job look like?
options: Leave it alone, since the customer only called about the toilet
Tell them they need a new unit today before it bursts on them
Tag the unit for follow-up and leave without mentioning it
Photograph both, show the customer and offer the four options
questions.why: A Service Tech diagnoses, fixes and sells on the spot. Show what you found and present the options so the customer can choose, without inflating the finding.

questions.q: You arrive at a Hornsby home to fix a dripping tap. Before you start, what's the best thing to tell the customer?
options: "I'll work it out as I go, and let you know what it all comes to once I'm done."
"I'll fix the tap, check the rest, then show you options before any extra work."
"I'll just get stuck in and fix whatever else I happen to find while I'm here."
"Tap jobs are quick, so I'll be in and out of here in ten minutes or so."
questions.why: Great service techs tell the customer what's going to happen: what they'll check, roughly how long, and that nothing extra happens until they've seen the options.

questions.q: A toilet in Epping keeps running and the inlet valve is clearly worn. What does the diagnostic flow say to do before you call it done?
options: Swap the valve and leave, since the cause is already obvious
Swap the valve and recommend a full re-pipe just to be safe
Test why it wore out, such as the pressure, then check the rest
Quote a new toilet suite, since worn valves always fail again
questions.why: Listen, inspect, test, find the root cause, then explain. A worn valve can be a symptom of high mains pressure, and fixing only the symptom means another call-out.

questions.q: During the health check at a Thornleigh home, the owner admits she has no idea where the stop tap is. What's the best move?
options: Show her where it is and how to turn it off in an emergency
Note it in the job and move on, since it isn't today's problem
Quote a replacement stop tap so it's easier for her to find
Suggest she rings the office later to ask where it is
questions.why: The health check includes whether the customer can find and turn off the stop tap in an emergency. Showing her takes a minute and could save her home.

questions.q: In Dulwich Hill the kitchen sink is blocked, the shower is draining slowly, and the ground around the gully grate is wet. Where's the blockage most likely to be?
options: The main line, rather than the sink trap
The kitchen sink trap, so plunge it first
The shower waste, so clear that first
The stormwater, so check the downpipes
questions.why: One fixture blocked points to that fixture's branch. Several fixtures affected, or the gully overflowing, points to the main line.

questions.q: A Beecroft sewer has blocked three times this year. The customer wants it "just cleared again, cheaply", and you suspect the pipe is cracked. What do you do?
options: Force the cutter through hard to clear it fast and keep it cheap
Clear it and leave, since that's exactly what the customer asked for
Recommend dig and replace straight away, without running the camera
Run the camera, show the footage and present all four options
questions.why: Run the camera first if you suspect damage, because forcing a cutter can make it worse. A clear is temporary with roots or damage present, so show the footage and let the customer choose, Elite first, without pressure.

questions.q: A customer in Pennant Hills has a water bill that's suddenly jumped, with no sign of a leak anywhere. Where do you start?
options: Open the wall behind the most likely fixture and have a look
Run a meter test first, recording readings, times and photos
Use the thermal camera and mark the leak wherever it shows warm
Tell them it's probably the meter and suggest they call Sydney Water
questions.why: The meter test proves whether water is escaping, so it comes first on every leak job. Thermal images are clues, not findings, and you never open a wall on a guess.

questions.q: After a night of storms in Wahroonga, a customer asks you to write that the leak "only started last night" so their insurance claim goes through. You can see old staining and mould. What do you write?
options: What they asked, since it helps the customer with their claim
That their insurer is unlikely to cover a leak like this one
Only what you saw, including the staining and the mould
Nothing at all, so the assessor can decide everything themselves
questions.why: Never change a finding to help a claim, and never tell a customer what their insurer will cover. Record exactly what you saw: an honest record protects the customer, the business and you.

questions.q: An elderly couple in Carlingford have had no hot water since last night. Their electric unit is eleven years old and the element has failed. What do you present?
options: Just the new element, since they're elderly and likely on a budget
Just a new unit, since repairing an old unit is a waste of money
Repair and replacement across all four options, Elite first
Nothing yet; tell them to ring the office for a replacement quote
questions.why: For older units, present repair vs replace across the four options, Elite first, and never prejudge what they can afford. If they choose a replacement, sell it on the spot.

questions.q: In Baulkham Hills, the hot water relief valve keeps running onto the path, and the customer asks you to cap it. What do you do?
options: Explain it's a safety device, then test the mains pressure
Cap it as asked, since a little water on the path isn't worth the fuss
Replace the relief valve and tell them that has fixed it for good
Plug the drain line so the water stops running across the path
questions.why: Never plug, cap or disable a relief valve. A constant flow often comes from high mains pressure, which a new valve alone won't fix but a pressure-limiting valve will.

questions.q: In Ryde, the customer says this is the third cistern inlet valve in two years. What's your next step?
options: Fit a new valve and tell them the last brand was the problem
Fit a more expensive valve so this one lasts a bit longer
Recommend a new toilet suite, since the cistern is worn out
Test the mains pressure, as repeat failures often point to it
questions.why: If the same kind of part keeps failing in a house, test the pressure. The valve fixes today; a PRV fixes the pattern.

questions.q: A tired old mixer in Hurstville needs a cartridge you don't carry for that brand. What's the best way to avoid a return trip?
options: Book a return visit straight away and leave the tap dripping for now
Offer the options, including a new mixer you carry, from the pricebook
Fit a cartridge from another brand that roughly fits, just for now
Order the cartridge and come back later without telling dispatch
questions.why: A return trip doubles the cost of the job. Offer an upgrade you do carry alongside the other options and let the customer choose, and never leave a bodge behind.

questions.q: In Westmead, a customer says, "Just fix the leak. I don't want to be sold anything." What's the best approach?
options: Present all four options before you start anyway, Elite first
Fix the leak and leave without mentioning anything else you saw
Fix the leak, then warn them the other problems are urgent
Fix the leak, then offer to show a couple of photos you took
questions.why: Respect what they asked for: fix it, then briefly show what you found. If they want to know more, present the options with no pressure.

questions.q: At a Dundas home for a running toilet, the health check finds a dripping shower mixer and perished flexi hoses. The customer asks if you'll "do a deal" for doing it all at once. What's right?
options: Take 10% off the Elite option, since it's a much bigger job
Quote only the toilet for now, so the price stays low and simple
Explain every line is pricebook; cheaper means fewer lines
Say you'll ask Harriet for a bundle price and call them back
questions.why: Bundle what you found into Standard, Premium and Elite, but never discount a bundle. If they want it cheaper, they choose an option with fewer lines.

questions.q: After fixing a shower mixer in Kellyville, you mention the Care Plan. The customer asks, "Does it cover parts?" You're not sure. What do you say?
options: That it's a good question, and you'll check and get back to them
Yes, since most memberships cover parts as well as labour
No, so that you can't be accused of overpromising anything
That they should look it up on the website, as it's not your area
questions.why: Never promise a benefit that isn't on the approved list. A confident guess that turns out wrong is the quickest way to lose a member.

questions.q: You've finished a quick tap washer job for a customer in a modest home in Auburn. Do you offer the Care Plan?
options: No, it's really only worth offering on the bigger jobs
Yes, briefly, as on every completed job, and a no is fine
No, they don't look like they'd be interested in a membership
Yes, and keep explaining the benefits until they agree to join
questions.why: The Care Plan is offered on every completed job, to every customer. Offered to some and not others, it becomes a judgement about them. The habit is the offer, not the sale.

questions.q: At 9pm in Kogarah, water is pouring through a kitchen ceiling and the customer's first question is what it will cost. What do you do?
options: Explain the after-hours pricing in full before you touch a single thing
Say "Let me stop the water first" and go straight to the stop tap
Photograph all the damage first so it's ready for the insurer
Ask them to sign an estimate before you turn anything off
questions.why: Make safe first: isolate, contain, protect, before the quote, the photos or the conversation about rates. Nothing calms a panicking customer faster than the water stopping.

questions.q: You've made safe a burst copper pipe under a house in Turramurra and presented four options for the permanent fix. She's rattled and wants to sleep on it. What do you do?
options: Start the re-pipe tonight, since it's clearly what the house needs
Warn her more bursts are coming unless she signs before you go
Leave without a plan, since she can always call if it bursts again
Agree a time to call her tomorrow and log it in ServiceTitan
questions.why: Let the customer choose with no pressure. If they're too rattled to decide tonight, agree when you'll follow up and log it in ServiceTitan.

questions.q: The hot water has failed at a rental in Merrylands, and the fix costs more than the property manager's approval limit. The tenant says, "Just fix it. The agent won't mind." What do you do?
options: Make safe, send the PM photos and options, and get it in writing
Do the full repair, since the tenant's OK covers it on a rental
Fit a cheaper fix that fits under the limit, even if it won't last
Ask the tenant to pay whatever the fix costs above the limit
questions.why: Tenants aren't the decision-maker. Never exceed the PM's approval limit without written approval, and never squeeze in a fix that won't solve the problem or ask the tenant to pay.

questions.q: Water is coming through the bathroom ceiling of a unit in Zetland. The tenant is sure it's the unit upstairs and asks who'll be paying. What do you do?
options: Tell them strata will pay, since the water is coming from above
Tell them the owner upstairs is responsible and has to fix it
Record exactly where it's coming through, with photos, and not guess
Go up and check the unit above yourself, even without access arranged
questions.why: Always record the facts about lot vs common property, but who approves and pays isn't your call on site. Never enter another lot without permission and arranged access.
